notes.title: Concept - What Is an LLM Agent
notes.scope: Defines the LLM agent and the autonomy spectrum from single prompt to fully autonomous loop, and settles the agent-vs-workflow distinction. IN: what makes something an agent, the component anatomy, when you should NOT build one. OUT: the loop internals (link Deep Dive - The Agent Loop) and tool mechanics (link Concept - Tool Use and Function Calling).
key_points: Anthropic's operative definition (Building Effective Agents, Dec 2024): workflows = LLMs orchestrated through predefined code paths; agents = LLM dynamically directs its own process and tool usage; the line is who controls the control flow
Agent anatomy: model + tool set + a loop + a termination condition + accumulated context/memory; strip any one and it is not an agent
The autonomy ladder: single call -> prompt chain -> router -> tool-use loop -> autonomous multi-step agent; each rung trades predictability for flexibility

The reliability tax: autonomy compounds per-step error (foreshadow p^n from Concept - Long-Horizon Agency and Error Compounding); a workflow that works is almost always cheaper, faster, and more debuggable
Decision heuristic: use an agent only when the task is open-ended and the steps cannot be hardcoded in advance; otherwise use a fixed workflow
Historical archetype: AutoGPT/BabyAGI (2023) as the first viral autonomous agents and cautionary tale (link Lore - The AutoGPT Explosion)
links: Concept - Tool Use and Function Calling
Concept - Chain-of-Thought and Why It Works
Concept - Cost Engineering for LLM Applications

notes.title: Reference - Agent Framework Landscape
notes.scope: A lookup matrix of the major agent frameworks/SDKs and their design paradigms as of 2026, for orientation and shortlisting. IN: what each framework is and its control model. OUT: the actual choose-one decision logic (link Decision - Choosing an Agent Framework).
key_points: Rows: LangGraph (graph/state-machine, low-level control, durable execution), OpenAI Agents SDK (Swarm successor, handoffs + guardrails), Anthropic Claude Agent SDK, CrewAI (role-based crews), AutoGen/AG2 (conversational multi-agent), LlamaIndex Workflows (event-driven), Hugging Face smolagents (code-as-action), Pydantic AI (type-safe outputs), DSPy (compile/optimize prompts), Google ADK
Columns: control paradigm, multi-agent support, streaming, human-in-the-loop, state/checkpoint persistence, provider lock-in, primary language, best-fit use case
Code-as-action distinction: smolagents/CodeAct emit Python instead of JSON tool calls; fewer round-trips, but requires a sandbox (link Checklist - Sandboxing an Agent)
DSPy is orthogonal: it optimizes prompts/weights rather than being a runtime loop; can wrap the others
Volatility warning: this table churns quarterly (Swarm->Agents SDK, HTTP+SSE->Streamable HTTP); date-stamp every row (as of 2026) and note deprecations
The raw-API baseline row: for a simple tool loop you often need no framework at all (link Playbook - Building a Tool-Use Agent from Scratch)
links: Playbook - Building a Tool-Use Agent from Scratch
Concept - Cost Engineering for LLM Applications

notes.title: Deep Dive - The Agent Loop
notes.scope: The full walkthrough of the agent control loop from the ReAct lineage to modern native-tool-calling agents. IN: the observe-think-act cycle, control/termination logic, context accumulation, and evolution of the loop. OUT: the atomic ReAct technique itself (link Concept - The ReAct Pattern) and tool-call wire formats (link Concept - Tool Use and Function Calling).
key_points: The loop: receive goal -> model emits reasoning + action (tool call or final answer) -> harness executes tool -> append observation as a tool message -> repeat until a stop condition; a diagram (Mermaid) tracing one full iteration is required

Termination logic: model stops by emitting no tool call / a final message; guard rails are max_iterations (typical 10-50) and a token/time budget; who owns the stop decision is the central design choice
Context accumulation: the transcript grows every turn (system/user/assistant/tool roles); tokens and cost scale with history (link Concept - Context Engineering for Agents, Concept - KV Cache)
Evolution: text-parsed ReAct (2022) -> native structured function calling -> parallel tool calls -> interleaved extended-thinking + tool use; each removed a class of parsing failure
Failure modes: infinite/oscillating loops, premature giving-up, context overflow mid-task, unhandled tool errors that the model does not notice
Prefix stability matters for economics: reordering messages busts prompt caching (link Concept - Prompt Caching); append-only transcripts preserve cache hits
The loop is model-agnostic scaffolding, but frontier models increasingly internalize parts of it (link Concept - Trained vs Prompted Agents)
links: Concept - Tool Use and Function Calling
Concept - Chain-of-Thought and Why It Works

notes.title: Concept - Tool Use and Function Calling
notes.scope: How an LLM invokes external functions: schemas in, structured calls out, results back in the loop. IN: the request/response mechanics, wire formats, tool-choice control, and why tool definitions dominate quality. OUT: the MCP standard (link Concept - Model Context Protocol (MCP)), robust parsing code (link Snippet - A Minimal ReAct Loop), and the pitfalls aggregate (link Gotchas - Tool Use and Function Calling).
key_points: Mechanism: developer supplies tool schemas (JSON Schema for parameters); model emits a structured call (name + argument object); harness executes and returns a tool/tool_result message keyed by call id
Wire formats differ: OpenAI tools/tool_calls array, Anthropic tool_use/tool_result content blocks; both are JSON but the framing and ids differ (link Reference - Agent Framework Landscape)
Under the hood the decoder is constrained/grammar-guided to emit schema-valid JSON (link Concept - Constrained Decoding); models are post-trained on tool-call traces to do this natively
tool_choice control: auto (model decides), required/any (must call something), or a named tool (force one); forcing is the fix for a model that narrates instead of acting
Parallel tool calls: modern models emit several calls in one turn for independent actions; the harness must fan out and return all results before the next turn

The model only sees names, descriptions, and param descriptions -- not your code; description quality and enum-over-freestring design determine tool-selection accuracy (link Checklist - Agent Tool Definition Review)
Selection degrades as tool count grows (historically past ~20-40 tools); mitigations: retrieval over tools, namespacing, sub-agents
Failure modes: hallucinated tool names, malformed/typed-wrong args, ignoring available tools, oversized results eating context
links: Gotchas - Tool Use and Function Calling

notes.title: Concept - Model Context Protocol (MCP)
notes.scope: The open protocol standardizing how applications expose tools, data, and prompts to LLMs. IN: the client/server architecture, the primitive set, transports, and the M+N integration argument. OUT: writing a server (link Snippet - Building an MCP Server) and injection/exfiltration risk theory (link Concept - Prompt Injection, Concept - The Lethal Trifecta for Agents).
key_points: Origin and pitch: Anthropic open-sourced MCP (Nov 2024) as an open standard; the USB-C-for-AI framing; adopted by OpenAI and Google DeepMind through 2025
Architecture: host application embeds an MCP client that speaks JSON-RPC 2.0 to one or more MCP servers; clean separation of the LLM app from integrations

Primitives: Tools (model-controlled functions), Resources (application-controlled data/context), Prompts (user-controlled templates), plus Sampling (server requests an LLM completion from the client), Roots, and Elicitation
Transports: stdio for local servers; Streamable HTTP (2025 spec) which replaced the older HTTP+SSE transport for remote servers
The economic argument: M hosts x N integrations collapses to M+N; a shared server ecosystem instead of bespoke glue per app

Security surface: tool descriptions are attacker-controlled text fed to the model (tool poisoning, rug-pull updates), over-permissioned servers, confused-deputy exfiltration (link Concept - The Lethal Trifecta for Agents)
Tool docstrings/descriptions are the model-facing contract, so a badly documented MCP tool is a badly performing one (link Checklist - Agent Tool Definition Review)
links: Concept - Tool Use and Function Calling
Concept - The Lethal Trifecta for Agents
Concept - Cost Engineering for LLM Applications

notes.title: Concept - The ReAct Pattern
notes.scope: The seminal reasoning-and-acting technique that interleaves thought, action, and observation. IN: the mechanism, why interleaving beats CoT-only and act-only, and the prompt format. OUT: the general loop scaffolding (link Deep Dive - The Agent Loop) and tree search over reasoning (link Concept - Search and Backtracking in Agents).
key_points: ReAct (Yao et al. 2022, Synergizing Reasoning and Acting): the model alternates Thought -> Action -> Observation traces in a single generation stream
Why it works: reasoning traces decompose the task and track progress; actions ground the reasoning in external observations, sharply reducing the hallucination that plagues CoT-only agents
Empirical contrast: on HotpotQA, Fever, ALFWorld, and WebShop, ReAct beats both act-only (no planning) and CoT-only (no grounding, hallucinates facts)

Original implementation used few-shot exemplars with hand-written thought/action strings and brittle text parsing; modern practice replaces the Action line with native tool calling (link Concept - Tool Use and Function Calling)
The thought tokens are a cheap scratchpad but a double-edged one: reasoning can also rationalize and entrench a wrong action, causing action loops
Failure modes: repeating the same failing action, looping between two states, thoughts that justify rather than diagnose
Reflexion (link Concept - Reflection and Self-Correction) extends ReAct by adding an inter-episode verbal-feedback memory
links: Concept - Tool Use and Function Calling
Concept - Chain-of-Thought and Why It Works
Concept - Search and Backtracking in Agents

notes.title: Concept - Task Decomposition and Planning
notes.scope: How agents break a goal into subtasks and sequence them: plan-first vs interleaved, and the named planning methods. IN: decomposition strategies, DAG planners, replanning. OUT: search/backtracking over plans (link Concept - Search and Backtracking in Agents) and multi-agent decomposition (link Pattern - Orchestrator-Worker Agents).
key_points: Two regimes: plan-then-execute (produce a full plan upfront, then run it) vs interleaved (ReAct-style, decide next action each turn); upfront plans are cheaper in LLM calls but brittle to surprises

Named methods: Least-to-Most prompting, Plan-and-Solve, decomposed prompting; ReWOO (Reasoning WithOut Observation) plans all tool calls upfront to cut token cost; LLMCompiler builds a task DAG and executes independent nodes in parallel (~1.8-3.7x latency speedup)
Router-style planning: HuggingGPT-style planners that select which tool/model handles each subtask
Hierarchical planning: a high-level plan whose steps are themselves decomposed on demand
Replanning: detecting that the plan no longer fits reality and regenerating; the key robustness lever for long tasks
Failure modes: over-planning (elaborate plans that die on contact with the environment), plans that ignore observed failures, dependency errors when parallelizing
When planning helps: tasks with clear stable structure; when it hurts: highly reactive/uncertain environments where interleaved wins
links: Concept - Search and Backtracking in Agents
Concept - Chain-of-Thought and Why It Works

notes.title: Pattern - Agentic Workflow Building Blocks
notes.scope: The reusable composition patterns for LLM systems short of full autonomy, per Anthropic's taxonomy. IN: augmented LLM, prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, evaluator-optimizer, and when to reach for each. OUT: the dynamic orchestrator-worker blueprint (link Pattern - Orchestrator-Worker Agents) and the autonomous loop (link Deep Dive - The Agent Loop).
key_points: Source taxonomy: Anthropic 'Building Effective Agents' (Dec 2024): augmented LLM (retrieval + tools + memory) as the base unit, then five composition patterns
Prompt chaining: decompose into fixed sequential LLM steps with optional gates between them; use when the task splits cleanly into stable subtasks
Routing: a classifier LLM dispatches inputs to specialized downstream handlers; use for heterogeneous inputs with distinct handling
Parallelization: sectioning (split into independent subtasks run concurrently) and voting (run the same task N times and aggregate); trades tokens for latency/reliability
Evaluator-optimizer: one LLM generates, another critiques against criteria, loop until acceptance; only helps when the evaluator has real signal (link Concept - Reflection and Self-Correction)
A diagram per pattern is required; each pattern names >=2 real uses

Design rule of thumb: prefer the most constrained pattern that works; escalate to an autonomous agent only when the control flow genuinely cannot be predetermined (link Concept - What Is an LLM Agent)
links: Concept - What Is an LLM Agent
Concept - Cost Engineering for LLM Applications

notes.title: Playbook - Building a Tool-Use Agent from Scratch
notes.scope: End-to-end procedure to build a working tool-use agent on the raw model API with no framework. IN: defining tools, the loop, dispatch, error handling, termination, and tracing. OUT: framework-specific setup (link Reference - Agent Framework Landscape) and sandboxing hardening (link Checklist - Sandboxing an Agent).
key_points: Prereqs: a model API with tool calling, 1-3 real tools, and a task that needs >1 step

Steps in order: (1) write tool schemas + handlers, (2) system prompt stating role and stopping rule, (3) the loop: call model -> if tool_calls, dispatch each and append tool results keyed by id -> else return final, (4) add max_iterations + token budget, (5) wrap handlers so exceptions return as tool-result error strings the model can read, (6) log every turn
Expected observation per step and what deviation means (e.g., model never calls the tool -> description or tool_choice problem)
Verification: run a task requiring two dependent tool calls; inspect the trace for correct id matching and a clean stop

When-it-goes-wrong branch table: infinite loop -> cap iterations + detect repeated calls; malformed args -> validate and echo the error back; stalls waiting -> a tool_result is missing for an emitted call; premature stop -> tighten the stopping instruction
Ties directly to Snippet - A Minimal ReAct Loop as the concrete code
Observability hook: emit structured spans per tool call for later debugging (link Concept - LLM Observability and Tracing)
links: Concept - Tool Use and Function Calling
Gotchas - Tool Use and Function Calling

notes.title: Snippet - A Minimal ReAct Loop
notes.scope: A complete, runnable ~50-line tool-use agent loop in Python demonstrating the core mechanics. IN: tool definition, the loop, tool-call dispatch, id matching, and safe error handling. OUT: framework abstractions and MCP (link Snippet - Building an MCP Server).
key_points: Complete runnable file: imports, one or two toy tools (e.g., a calculator and a web-search stub), schema definitions, and the loop against a real SDK (anthropic or openai)
Header block: dependencies with versions (e.g., anthropic>=0.40 or openai>=1.40), how to set the API key, and the expected multi-turn trace output

Demonstrate the three load-bearing details: a max_iterations guard, appending each tool_result with its matching tool_use_id/tool_call_id, and returning handler exceptions as tool-result error text rather than raising
Show the stop condition: loop exits when the model returns a message with no tool calls
Keep it framework-free so the mechanics are visible; comments only where the SDK shape is non-obvious
Why-it-is-written-this-way section covers: id matching (mismatches error the API), error-as-observation (lets the model self-correct), and the iteration cap (prevents runaway cost)
links: Concept - Tool Use and Function Calling
Playbook - Building a Tool-Use Agent from Scratch
Gotchas - Tool Use and Function Calling

notes.title: Checklist - Agent Tool Definition Review
notes.scope: A pre-flight review for any tool exposed to an agent, since the model acts only on the schema it sees. IN: naming, descriptions, parameter design, return shape, and safety gating of a single tool. OUT: sandboxing the runtime (link Checklist - Sandboxing an Agent) and the wider production pitfalls (link Gotchas - Agents in Production).
key_points: Naming: verb-noun, unambiguous, non-overlapping with sibling tools so the model does not confuse them
Description states both when to use AND when not to use the tool, with a short example invocation
Every parameter has a description with units/format; prefer enums over free strings; required-vs-optional is set correctly and defaults are documented
Returns are concise and structured, and token-budgeted -- a tool that returns 10k tokens of JSON will crowd out the transcript
Errors return actionable, model-readable messages (what to do next), never raw stack traces
Side effects and idempotency are declared; destructive/irreversible actions are gated behind confirmation or a human-in-the-loop step
Token cost of the schema itself is measured (many tools multiply system-prompt size)
Why-these-items ties each to a real failure: vague description -> wrong tool picked; unhelpful error text -> agent loops; verbose return -> context blowout; ungated destructive op -> data loss
links: Concept - Tool Use and Function Calling
Gotchas - Tool Use and Function Calling
Playbook - Building a Tool-Use Agent from Scratch

notes.title: Decision - Choosing an Agent Framework
notes.scope: The choose-one decision among raw API and the major agent frameworks, with the constraints that flip it. IN: decision flow and tradeoff matrix across control, velocity, and lock-in. OUT: the descriptive per-framework feature list (link Reference - Agent Framework Landscape) and single-vs-multi-agent topology (link Decision - Single-Agent vs Multi-Agent).
key_points: Decision flow (Mermaid): first ask whether you need a framework at all -- a simple tool loop is often best on the raw provider SDK; escalate only when a real need appears

Branch by need: explicit state/graph control and durable execution -> LangGraph; heavy multi-agent conversation -> AutoGen/CrewAI; type-safe validated outputs -> Pydantic AI; prompt/weight optimization -> DSPy; provider-native handoffs -> OpenAI Agents SDK / Claude Agent SDK
Tradeoff matrix columns: control granularity, time-to-first-agent, debuggability, streaming + human-in-the-loop support, state persistence/checkpointing, and vendor lock-in

Details that flip the default: need to pause/resume or replay runs (durable execution favors LangGraph/Temporal-style); need code-as-action (smolagents) with a sandbox; regulatory need for full trace control (thin raw-API stack)
Default for 2026: start on the raw provider SDK for a single-tool-loop agent; adopt LangGraph when you genuinely need explicit state, branching, and checkpoints
Anti-pattern: adopting a heavy multi-agent framework before proving a single agent cannot do the job (link Decision - Single-Agent vs Multi-Agent)
links: Playbook - Building a Tool-Use Agent from Scratch
Concept - Cost Engineering for LLM Applications

notes.title: Concept - Agent Memory Systems
notes.scope: How agents persist and retrieve information beyond the context window: the memory taxonomy and the retrieval/writing mechanisms. IN: short vs long-term, episodic/semantic/procedural memory, scoring and self-editing memory. OUT: vector index internals (link Concept - HNSW, Concept - Embedding Models) and transcript compaction (link Concept - Context Engineering for Agents).
key_points: Taxonomy: short-term/working memory = the context window; long-term = an external store; by content type: episodic (past interactions), semantic (facts about the world/user), procedural (learned skills/how-to)

Generative Agents (Park et al. 2023): a memory stream scored by retrieval = recency (exponential decay) + importance (LLM-rated) + relevance (embedding similarity); plus periodic reflection that synthesizes higher-level memories
MemGPT / Letta (Packer et al. 2023): OS-inspired virtual context -- a limited main context plus external storage, with the model self-editing memory via function calls and paging data in/out
Write policy is the hard part: deciding what is worth storing, deduping, and reconciling contradictions; naive 'embed everything' produces low-signal recall
Retrieval of memories reuses RAG machinery (link Concept - Embedding Models, Concept - HNSW, Concept - Rerankers) but the query is agent-generated, not user-typed
Failure modes: memory bloat, stale/contradictory memories surfacing, retrieval misses on paraphrase, and over-writing that erases still-relevant facts
Distinction from context engineering: memory is the durable external store; context engineering is managing what currently sits in the window (link Concept - Context Engineering for Agents)

notes.title: Concept - Multi-Agent Orchestration
notes.scope: How multiple LLM agents are coordinated: topologies, communication, and when multi beats single. IN: orchestrator/hierarchical/debate topologies, message passing, cost and coordination tradeoffs. OUT: the concrete orchestrator-worker blueprint (link Pattern - Orchestrator-Worker Agents) and the go/no-go choice (link Decision - Single-Agent vs Multi-Agent).
key_points: Topologies: single orchestrator + worker subagents, hierarchical trees, sequential pipelines, group chat/debate, and free-form networks
Communication mechanisms: a shared scratchpad/blackboard, explicit message passing, and handoffs (OpenAI Swarm/Agents SDK transfer semantics)

When multi-agent helps: parallelizable, separable subtasks and context isolation (each subagent gets a clean window); Anthropic reported multi-agent research beating single-agent by ~90% on an internal eval
The cost multiplier: Anthropic measured ~15x the tokens of a chat interaction, and token volume explained ~80% of performance variance -- multi-agent buys capability by spending tokens
When it hurts: coordination overhead, error propagation across agents, diffusion of responsibility, and write-conflicts when agents edit shared state (Cognition's 'Don't Build Multi-Agents', 2025)
Research lineage: multi-agent debate (Du et al. 2023), CAMEL role-play, Society-of-Mind style ensembles
Evaluation is harder: non-determinism and long trajectories make multi-agent runs hard to score reproducibly (link Concept - Agent Evaluation Challenges)
links: Concept - Cost Engineering for LLM Applications

notes.title: Gotchas - Agents in Production
notes.scope: The aggregated production failure modes of autonomous agents, ordered by how much pain they cause. IN: loops, cost/context blowups, silent failures, injection-driven exfiltration, latency, and irreversibility. OUT: tool-call-specific bugs (link Gotchas - Tool Use and Function Calling) and injection taxonomy (link Concept - Prompt Injection).
key_points: Infinite/oscillating tool loops: symptom repeated identical calls; cause the model rationalizing a failing action; fix iteration caps + loop detection + returning richer error observations
Context window overflow mid-task: cause unbounded transcript growth; fix compaction, sub-agent isolation, scratchpad offload (link Concept - Context Engineering for Agents)
Cost blowup: per-turn token growth multiplied by turns and (for multi-agent) ~15x fan-out; detection = per-run token/cost budgets and alerts (link Concept - Cost Engineering for LLM Applications)
Silent tool failures: the tool errored but the model did not notice and proceeds on a false premise; fix explicit error signaling and post-conditions
Prompt-injection-driven exfiltration from web/tool/email content -- the lethal trifecta (link Concept - The Lethal Trifecta for Agents, Concept - Prompt Injection)
Latency compounding: N sequential model calls stack end-to-end; mitigate with parallelization and speculative steps
Over-eager destructive actions with no rollback; goal drift on long runs (fix: recitation of the goal/todo each turn); non-determinism making evals flaky
Detection backbone: trace-level observability on every tool call is the single highest-leverage investment (link Concept - LLM Observability and Tracing)
links: Gotchas - Tool Use and Function Calling
Concept - The Lethal Trifecta for Agents
Concept - Cost Engineering for LLM Applications
Concept - Long-Horizon Agency and Error Compounding

notes.title: Gotchas - Tool Use and Function Calling
notes.scope: The specific pitfalls of the tool-calling interface, ordered by frequency and pain. IN: schema/argument bugs, selection degradation, id and parallel-call bugs, result-formatting traps. OUT: broader production/agent-lifecycle failures (link Gotchas - Agents in Production) and defining tools well (link Checklist - Agent Tool Definition Review).
key_points: Malformed or wrongly-typed arguments (string '5' vs int 5, missing required field); cause weak schema/description; fix strict validation + constrained decoding (link Concept - Constrained Decoding)
Tool-selection degradation with too many tools: past a few dozen the model picks wrong; fix namespacing, retrieval-over-tools, or sub-agents
Ambiguous/overlapping descriptions -> wrong tool chosen; fix disambiguating 'use when / do not use when' language
tool_call_id / tool_use_id mismatches: a returned result not keyed to its call errors the API or confuses the model
Parallel tool calls with hidden data dependencies executed out of order; fix declaring dependencies or forcing sequential calls
Oversized tool results eating the context window; fix truncation/summarization and pagination of tool output
Missing tool result -> the model stalls waiting; the model narrating an action instead of emitting a call -> fix with tool_choice forcing
Injection via attacker-controlled tool descriptions/results (link Concept - The Lethal Trifecta for Agents)
links: Concept - Tool Use and Function Calling
Concept - The Lethal Trifecta for Agents

notes.title: Concept - Reflection and Self-Correction
notes.scope: How agents critique and revise their own outputs, and the sharp limit on when this actually helps. IN: Reflexion, Self-Refine, tool-augmented critique, and the internal-vs-external-signal boundary. OUT: the evaluator-optimizer workflow shape (link Pattern - Agentic Workflow Building Blocks) and RL-trained self-correction (link Concept - Trained vs Prompted Agents).
key_points: Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023): after a failed episode the agent writes a verbal self-reflection into memory and retries; improves ALFWorld/HumanEval by learning across attempts without weight updates
Self-Refine (Madaan et al. 2023): single-episode iterative self-feedback and revision
CRITIC and tool-augmented correction: the model verifies claims with external tools (search, code execution) before revising

The critical limit: Huang et al. 2023 ('LLMs Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet') show that without an external signal, self-correction of reasoning can leave quality flat or worse -- the model cannot reliably find its own reasoning errors
So reflection pays off when there is a ground-truth oracle: unit tests, a compiler, a checker, or retrieved evidence; it degrades when purely introspective
Failure modes: reflections that rationalize the original answer, oscillation between two answers, and the token/latency cost of extra passes
Practical corollary: wire a verifier into the loop rather than trusting the model to grade itself (link Concept - GRPO and RL with Verifiable Rewards for the trained analogue)
links: Concept - GRPO and RL with Verifiable Rewards
Concept - Chain-of-Thought and Why It Works
Concept - Long-Horizon Agency and Error Compounding

notes.title: Concept - Context Engineering for Agents
notes.scope: Managing what sits in an agent's context window across a long run, distinct from durable memory. IN: compaction, scratchpad/filesystem offload, sub-agent isolation, cache-friendly layout, just-in-time loading. OUT: the general context-rot mechanism (link Concept - Context Rot) and the external memory store (link Concept - Agent Memory Systems).
key_points: The core problem: agent transcripts grow every turn, so quality degrades from context rot and lost-in-the-middle while cost scales with history length (link Concept - Context Rot)
Compaction: summarizing old turns to reclaim window; the risk is over-compaction dropping a fact the agent later needs

Offload to the environment: write notes/plans to a scratchpad or filesystem and re-read on demand instead of carrying everything in-context (Anthropic effective-context-engineering, 2025; Manus lessons)
Sub-agent context isolation: workers return distilled summaries, not their full trace, keeping the orchestrator window clean (link Pattern - Orchestrator-Worker Agents)

Cache-friendly layout: keep a stable append-only prefix so prompt caching / KV reuse stays hot; reordering or editing early messages busts the cache (link Concept - Prompt Caching, Concept - KV Cache)
Just-in-time retrieval: pull only the currently relevant history/documents into the window (link Deep Dive - RAG Architectures)
Tool-result hygiene: truncate/paginate large outputs before they enter the window
Failure modes: over-compaction amnesia, cache invalidation from reordering, and irrelevant history drowning the signal
links: Concept - Long-Horizon Agency and Error Compounding

notes.title: Concept - Computer Use and GUI Grounding
notes.scope: Agents that operate a computer or browser through screenshots and mouse/keyboard actions. IN: the action space, the pixel-to-coordinate grounding problem, and grounding techniques. OUT: VLM architecture internals (link Concept - VLM Architectures) and browser-side retrieval (link Deep Dive - RAG Architectures).
key_points: Setup: the agent observes screenshots and emits GUI actions -- click(x,y), type, scroll, keypress -- in a perceive-act loop; Anthropic Computer Use (Oct 2024) and OpenAI Operator/CUA (2025) are the reference systems
The grounding problem: mapping rendered pixels to a correct click coordinate is the bottleneck; small errors cause misclicks and cascade

Grounding techniques: Set-of-Marks prompting (overlay numbered labels on UI elements so the model names an element instead of guessing coordinates); the accessibility/DOM tree as a cheaper, more reliable action target when available; pure-vision grounding when it is not
Benchmarks: OSWorld (real desktop tasks), WebArena/VisualWebArena, ScreenSpot (grounding accuracy), WebVoyager; report metrics with dates
Numbers: early Claude computer use scored roughly the mid-teens on OSWorld vs ~72% human (late 2024), improving through 2025-26 but still far below human reliability
Failure modes: coordinate drift, misclicks, inability to perceive hover/transient states, and screenshot-loop latency making each step slow and expensive
Non-obvious: prefer the accessibility tree over vision whenever exposed; vision grounding is both the capability frontier and the main error source
links: Concept - Long-Horizon Agency and Error Compounding

notes.title: Pattern - Orchestrator-Worker Agents
notes.scope: The reusable design where a lead agent dynamically decomposes a task and spawns worker subagents, then synthesizes. IN: structure, context isolation, synthesis, cost forces, and known uses. OUT: the broader topology survey (link Concept - Multi-Agent Orchestration) and the specific Anthropic system (link Breakdown - Anthropic's Multi-Agent Research System).
key_points: Problem/solution: for open-ended tasks whose subtasks cannot be predetermined, a lead/orchestrator LLM decides at runtime how many workers to spawn and what each does, then merges results (contrast with static parallelization in Pattern - Agentic Workflow Building Blocks)
Structure (diagram required): orchestrator -> N workers with isolated contexts -> workers return distilled findings -> orchestrator synthesizes; effectively map-reduce over LLM calls
Context isolation is the key benefit: each worker gets a clean window on its subtask, sidestepping the single-agent context-rot ceiling
Implementation notes: the orchestrator prompt must specify how to delegate and how much effort to allocate (spawn count scaled to complexity); workers must return summaries, not full traces
Known uses: Anthropic's multi-agent research system, deep-research agents (OpenAI/Google 2025), large-scale document map-reduce

Tradeoffs / when NOT to use: heavy token cost (~15x), coordination and duplicated-work failures, and it breaks down when subtasks share mutable state or must write to a common artifact (favor single-agent then)
Pairs with a synthesis/evaluator step to reconcile conflicting worker outputs (link Concept - Reflection and Self-Correction)
links: Concept - Cost Engineering for LLM Applications

notes.title: Decision - Single-Agent vs Multi-Agent
notes.scope: When to split a task across multiple agents versus keeping one agent, with the tradeoffs that flip it. IN: decomposability test, read-vs-write distinction, cost/coordination matrix. OUT: how to wire the orchestration once chosen (link Concept - Multi-Agent Orchestration, Pattern - Orchestrator-Worker Agents).
key_points: Decision flow (Mermaid): is the task decomposable into subtasks with separable context and few write-dependencies? read-heavy parallel research favors multi; write-heavy shared-artifact work favors single

Tradeoff matrix: single-agent (simpler, cheaper, coherent shared context, but context-window-bound and serial) vs multi-agent (parallel, context isolation, but ~15x tokens, coordination failures, harder to evaluate)

The pivotal evidence pair: Anthropic's multi-agent research win (~90% over single on a research eval, 2025) for parallel read/breadth tasks vs Cognition's 'Don't Build Multi-Agents' (2025) arguing shared context and fragile coordination make multi-agent worse for coherent build/write tasks
The write-conflict problem: multiple agents editing shared state produce inconsistent results no synthesizer can cleanly merge
Default (2026): a single agent plus strong context engineering until you hit demonstrable, independent parallelism; do not reach for multi-agent to paper over a weak single-agent design
Cost gate: multi-agent must justify a several-fold token bill with a matching capability gain (link Concept - Cost Engineering for LLM Applications)
links: Concept - Cost Engineering for LLM Applications

notes.title: Checklist - Sandboxing an Agent
notes.scope: A pre-flight hardening list before granting an agent real tool access to systems, files, network, or credentials. IN: isolation, egress control, least privilege, approval gates, audit, kill switch. OUT: the injection theory itself (link Concept - Prompt Injection) and the exfiltration failure pattern (link Concept - The Lethal Trifecta for Agents).
key_points: Run in an isolated container/microVM (gVisor, Firecracker) rather than on the host; no host filesystem mounts, read-only where possible
Network egress on an allowlist -- the single most important control for preventing data exfiltration (link Concept - The Lethal Trifecta for Agents)
No ambient credentials/secrets in the environment; use short-lived scoped tokens and least-privilege identities per tool
Per-tool permission gating with human approval for destructive, irreversible, or exfil-capable actions
Resource limits: CPU/memory/wallclock/token budgets and rate limits on external calls to cap blast radius and cost
Treat every tool output (web page, file, email, MCP tool result) as untrusted input that may carry injection
Audit-log every tool call with arguments and results; provide a kill switch to halt a running agent
Why-these-items ties each to a real incident class: agent running rm -rf, secrets leaked via a web/search tool, and injection-to-exfiltration through untrusted content
links: Concept - The Lethal Trifecta for Agents
Concept - Computer Use and GUI Grounding

notes.title: Reference - Agent Benchmarks
notes.scope: A lookup matrix of the benchmarks used to measure agent capability, with what each tests and its flaws. IN: coding, web, computer-use, and tool-agent-user benchmarks with metrics and approximate SOTA (as of 2026). OUT: general eval methodology and statistics (link Deep Dive - Designing an Eval Harness, Concept - Statistical Rigor in Model Evaluation) and why agent eval is intrinsically hard (link Concept - Agent Evaluation Challenges).
key_points: Coding: SWE-bench (2,294 real GitHub issues), SWE-bench Verified (500 human-filtered), SWE-bench Multimodal; metric = % resolved by hidden tests (link Breakdown - SWE-bench and SWE-agent)
Web/browsing: WebArena, VisualWebArena, WebVoyager, BrowseComp (OpenAI 2025, hard retrieval-style browsing); metric = task success rate
General assistant: GAIA (Meta 2023, three difficulty levels of real multi-step tasks), AgentBench (multi-environment)
Tool-agent-user: tau-bench and tau2-bench (retail/airline, user-simulator in the loop) with the pass^k reliability metric = succeeding k independent times, not just once
Computer use: OSWorld (desktop), plus grounding sets like ScreenSpot; ML engineering: MLE-bench; security: Cybench; terminals: Terminal-Bench
Columns: domain, task count, metric (pass@1 vs pass^k), what it actually measures, known flaws/contamination, approximate top score (date-stamped as of 2026)

Footnote the metrics: pass@1 vs pass^k vs resolved-rate are not comparable; contamination is pervasive because many task sources predate model training cutoffs (link Concept - Benchmark Contamination)
links: Deep Dive - Designing an Eval Harness
Concept - Statistical Rigor in Model Evaluation

notes.title: Snippet - Building an MCP Server
notes.scope: A complete, runnable minimal MCP server exposing a tool and a resource over stdio, plus how a client connects. IN: server definition, tool/resource registration, transport, and the docstring-as-contract detail. OUT: the protocol concepts (link Concept - Model Context Protocol (MCP)) and security hardening (link Checklist - Sandboxing an Agent).
key_points: Runnable Python using the official MCP SDK (FastMCP): define one tool and one resource, run over stdio
Header block: dependencies with versions (mcp / modelcontextprotocol python-sdk), how to register the server in a host (e.g., Claude Desktop config), and expected behavior when the tool is called
Show that the tool's docstring/description becomes the model-facing contract -- the single highest-leverage line in the file (link Checklist - Agent Tool Definition Review)
Demonstrate a Resource (application-controlled data) alongside the Tool (model-controlled action) to make the primitive distinction concrete
Use typed function signatures so the SDK derives the JSON Schema automatically; return structured, concise results
Why-it-is-written-this-way: stdio for local dev vs Streamable HTTP for remote, typed args for schema generation, and error handling that returns model-readable messages
Note the trust boundary: a server's tool descriptions are attacker-controlled text if the server is third-party (link Concept - The Lethal Trifecta for Agents)
links: Concept - Tool Use and Function Calling

notes.title: Breakdown - SWE-bench and SWE-agent
notes.scope: How the SWE-bench benchmark is constructed and how SWE-agent's Agent-Computer Interface unlocked coding-agent performance. IN: benchmark construction, the ACI insight, headline numbers, and flaws. OUT: the full benchmark catalog (link Reference - Agent Benchmarks) and a shipped product agent (link Breakdown - Claude Code).
key_points: SWE-bench (Jimenez et al. 2023): 2,294 real issue+PR pairs from 12 popular Python repos; the agent must produce a patch that passes the PR's hidden tests; SWE-bench Verified (500, OpenAI 2024) is the human-filtered subset that removed under-specified/broken tasks
Headline trajectory: 2023 retrieval baselines ~2%; SWE-agent ~12%; by 2025-26 top agents reach 60-70%+ on Verified (date-stamped, as of 2026)

SWE-agent (Yang et al. 2024) key insight -- the Agent-Computer Interface: a purpose-built command set (open/scroll/search/edit files) with feedback on every action, including linting on edit; the ACI mattered more than raw model strength

The clever parts: design the interface for the model not the human, give feedback after every action, and use test-passing as a verifiable reward (RLVR-adjacent, link Concept - GRPO and RL with Verifiable Rewards)

What is dated/flawed: Python-only, tests-pass does not equal correct-fix, localization vs editing conflation, and contamination since issues predate training cutoffs (link Concept - Benchmark Contamination)
What to steal: invest in the tool/interface layer; wire verifiable checks into the loop; treat retrieval/localization as a first-class subproblem
Ties to the Devin controversy over how SWE-bench scores are reported (link Lore - The Devin Demo and the SWE-bench Reality Gap)
links: Concept - GRPO and RL with Verifiable Rewards
Lore - The Devin Demo and the SWE-bench Reality Gap

notes.title: Concept - Agent Evaluation Challenges
notes.scope: Why evaluating agents is uniquely hard compared to single-turn model eval, framed from the agent side. IN: outcome-vs-trajectory, non-determinism/variance, reproducibility, cost/latency as metrics, judging trajectories. OUT: general statistics and harness design (link Concept - Statistical Rigor in Model Evaluation, Deep Dive - Designing an Eval Harness) and the benchmark list (link Reference - Agent Benchmarks).
key_points: Outcome vs trajectory: a task can succeed while the path was unsafe, wasteful, or lucky; agent eval must score both the end state and the process

Non-determinism: the same task yields different trajectories run-to-run, producing high variance; single-seed scores are misleading, motivating pass^k reliability metrics (succeed k times) as in tau-bench
Environment reproducibility: agents touch live tools/web/state that drift, so a benchmark can silently change under you; sandboxed frozen environments are required for fair comparison
Cost and latency are first-class metrics, not footnotes -- an agent that solves a task at 15x tokens or 10x latency is a different product
Judging trajectories with an LLM inherits position/verbosity/self-preference biases (link Concept - LLM-as-Judge) and is harder over long multi-step traces
Long horizon breaks attribution: when a 30-step run fails, which step caused it is often ambiguous (link Concept - Long-Horizon Agency and Error Compounding)

Contamination and reward hacking: benchmark tasks leak into training and agents learn to game the metric (link Concept - Benchmark Contamination, Concept - Reward Hacking); METR-style time-horizon eval is an emerging alternative framing
links: Concept - Statistical Rigor in Model Evaluation
Deep Dive - Designing an Eval Harness
Concept - Long-Horizon Agency and Error Compounding

notes.title: Concept - Long-Horizon Agency and Error Compounding
notes.scope: Why agent success decays over long task horizons and what breaks or beats the decay. IN: the p^n compounding math, METR time-horizon measurement, correlated errors, and recovery. OUT: reflection mechanics (link Concept - Reflection and Self-Correction) and eval methodology (link Concept - Agent Evaluation Challenges).
key_points: The compounding math: with per-step success probability p and independent steps, an n-step task succeeds with ~p^n; p=0.95, n=20 gives ~0.36 -- exponential decay is why long autonomous runs fail
This is the mechanism behind the AutoGPT-era failures: 2023 models had per-step p too low for the horizons users attempted (link Lore - The AutoGPT Explosion)
METR (2025) 'Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks': define an agent's 50%-success task-length horizon; frontier horizon roughly doubling every ~7 months, reaching the order of hours by 2026
The independence assumption is wrong in both directions: correlated errors (one wrong belief poisons many steps) worsen decay, while detect-and-recover capability breaks the naive p^n and dominates
Practical corollary: an agent with slightly lower p but strong error-detection and recovery beats a higher-p agent that cannot notice it is off-track
Mitigations: checkpoints and verification between steps, decomposition into shorter verifiable subtasks, human-in-the-loop gates, and reducing per-step error (better tools/prompts)
The failure signature: the 'death spiral' where an agent that goes off-track compounds the error instead of recovering (link Gotchas - Agents in Production)

notes.title: Concept - Search and Backtracking in Agents
notes.scope: Explicit deliberate search over reasoning/action trajectories, beyond greedy ReAct, and why most production agents avoid it. IN: Tree of Thoughts, LATS/MCTS-for-agents, value functions, and the cost argument. OUT: linear planning (link Concept - Task Decomposition and Planning) and RL-internalized search (link Concept - Trained vs Prompted Agents, Concept - GRPO and RL with Verifiable Rewards).
key_points: Motivation: greedy ReAct commits to one path; deliberate search explores alternatives and backtracks from dead ends
Tree of Thoughts (Yao et al. 2023): frame reasoning as a tree, expand candidate thoughts, evaluate states with a value/self-eval, search via BFS/DFS

Language Agent Tree Search / LATS (Zhou et al. 2023): MCTS over ReAct nodes combining acting, a learned/self value estimate, and Reflexion-style feedback; RAP (Reasoning via Planning) is a related planner
Mechanism mapping: state = the agent trajectory so far, expansion = candidate next actions, evaluation = self-eval or environment reward, backtracking = abandon low-value branches
Why production mostly skips it: explicit search multiplies LLM calls (often 10-100x), exploding cost and latency; a strong single path plus reflection is usually the better tradeoff

The frontier shift: reasoning models (o-series, DeepSeek-R1) internalize search into a long chain-of-thought via RL, getting search-like benefits without an external tree (link Concept - GRPO and RL with Verifiable Rewards)
Failure mode: search guided by a bad value function just burns tokens exploring worthless branches
links: Concept - GRPO and RL with Verifiable Rewards
Concept - Chain-of-Thought and Why It Works
Concept - Cost Engineering for LLM Applications

notes.title: Concept - Trained vs Prompted Agents
notes.scope: The paradigm shift from prompt-scaffolded agents on frozen models to models RL-trained end-to-end for agentic behavior, framed from the agent-architecture side. IN: why scaffolding hits a ceiling, what end-to-end training changes, and environment design. OUT: the RL training mechanics themselves (link Concept - GRPO and RL with Verifiable Rewards, Deep Dive - RLHF End to End), owned by Post-Training.
key_points: The old paradigm: a frozen base model plus clever prompting/scaffolding (ReAct prompts, tool descriptions, orchestration); the new paradigm: RL-train the model directly on agentic tasks with verifiable rewards
Why the shift: scaffolding hits a ceiling because the base model was never optimized to use tools, recover from errors, or manage a long horizon; training teaches those behaviors into the weights

Evidence: o-series and Claude tool-use training, DeepSeek-R1's RL recipe; agents trained on SWE-gym / tau-bench-style environments; the mechanics live in Post-Training (link Concept - GRPO and RL with Verifiable Rewards)

Environment design becomes the work: define an agentic task distribution and a verifiable reward (tests pass, task-user satisfied), then RL against it -- the reward is the hard part (link Concept - Reward Hacking)

Consequence for architecture: the scaffold gets thinner as models improve -- Anthropic and Cognition both observe that heavy orchestration should shrink as the model absorbs agentic skill (link Breakdown - Claude Code)
Ownership boundary: this note frames the agent-domain implications; the PPO/GRPO/RLVR internals are Post-Training's
Open question: how much agentic capability can be scaffolded vs must be trained -- the moving line that determines framework value
links: Concept - GRPO and RL with Verifiable Rewards
Deep Dive - RLHF End to End
Concept - Search and Backtracking in Agents
Concept - Long-Horizon Agency and Error Compounding

notes.title: Breakdown - Anthropic's Multi-Agent Research System
notes.scope: How Anthropic's production multi-agent research system works and what its engineering write-up teaches about orchestrator-worker design. IN: architecture, the token/performance numbers, the clever prompt-engineering decisions, and the hard parts. OUT: the reusable pattern in the abstract (link Pattern - Orchestrator-Worker Agents) and the single-vs-multi decision (link Decision - Single-Agent vs Multi-Agent).
key_points: Source: Anthropic engineering blog 'How we built our multi-agent research system' (June 2025); a lead Claude orchestrator spawns parallel subagent researchers with isolated contexts and synthesizes their findings

Headline numbers: multi-agent beat single-agent by ~90% on an internal research eval; used ~15x the tokens of a chat interaction; token usage explained ~80% of performance variance across configurations

Clever parts: parallel subagents for breadth/coverage, per-subagent context isolation, an explicit orchestrator prompt teaching it how to delegate, and effort scaling (spawn subagent count proportional to query complexity)
Prompt-engineering lessons: teach the orchestrator to decompose and set clear subagent objectives; iterate prompts against evals because small wording changes shift delegation behavior
Hard parts / what they got wrong: subagents duplicating work, coordination overhead, evaluation difficulty under non-determinism, and the raw cost of the token multiplier
The contrast case: Cognition's 'Don't Build Multi-Agents' argues the opposite for write-heavy coherent tasks; both can be right by task type (link Decision - Single-Agent vs Multi-Agent)
What to steal: orchestrator-worker for breadth/research tasks, context isolation, and treating token budget as a capability dial
links: Concept - Cost Engineering for LLM Applications

notes.title: Breakdown - Claude Code
notes.scope: How Anthropic's terminal coding agent is architected, as a real-world instance of a thin-scaffold model-first agent. IN: the tool set, permission system, memory/subagents, and the design philosophy. OUT: the SWE-bench benchmark mechanics (link Breakdown - SWE-bench and SWE-agent) and generic sandboxing steps (link Checklist - Sandboxing an Agent).
key_points: What it is: Anthropic's CLI coding agent (2025) -- a single main agent loop wrapping a real model with a curated tool set, running in the user's terminal/repo

Tool set: file navigation via Grep/Glob (deliberately search-based, not embedding-RAG for code), Read/Edit/Write, Bash, WebFetch, a Task tool that spawns isolated subagents, and TodoWrite for long-task tracking
Permission system: allow/ask/deny per tool and per pattern, with human approval gates for destructive or out-of-scope actions -- security as UX, not just sandbox

Context handling: CLAUDE.md project memory files, context compaction on long sessions, and subagents with isolated windows to keep the main context clean (link Concept - Context Engineering for Agents)

Design philosophy: a deliberately thin/unopinionated scaffold -- give the model excellent tools and let it drive, rather than hardcoding complex orchestration; this reflects the trained-agent thesis (link Concept - Trained vs Prompted Agents)
The recitation trick made product: a live todo list re-surfaces the goal each turn to fight long-horizon drift (link Lore - Agent Prompt-Engineering Folklore)
What to steal: search-over-embeddings for code, permission gating, todo recitation, and thin scaffold + strong tools; limits: large-repo context bounds, cost, and over-eager edits
Evidence status: based on Anthropic's public materials and the observable tool surface of the product
links: Concept - Tool Use and Function Calling

notes.title: Lore - The AutoGPT Explosion
notes.scope: The March-April 2023 viral rise of AutoGPT/BabyAGI and why the first wave of autonomous agents mostly failed. IN: the story, the technical reasons for failure, and the durable lesson. OUT: the compounding math in full (link Concept - Long-Horizon Agency and Error Compounding) and modern loop design (link Deep Dive - The Agent Loop).
key_points: What happened: AutoGPT (Toran Bruce Richards) and BabyAGI (Yohei Nakajima) went viral in spring 2023; AutoGPT became one of the fastest repos to 100k+ GitHub stars; the pitch was fully autonomous GPT-4 agents that pursue a goal unsupervised; the ChaosGPT stunt amplified the hype

Why they mostly failed: GPT-4's per-step reliability was too low for the long horizons users attempted, so errors compounded (p^n, link Concept - Long-Horizon Agency and Error Compounding); naive vector-dump 'memory' gave poor recall; agents fell into infinite loops, hallucinated task completion, and burned real API money getting stuck

The lesson (mechanical): autonomy needs a per-step reliability the 2023 base models did not have; scaffolding cannot rescue a model whose step-error is too high; memory needs a write/retrieval policy, not just an embedding dump
The legacy: AutoGPT seeded the entire agent-framework wave and set expectations that models only grew into over the following two years
Partial vindication: the same architecture works far better on 2025-26 models because per-step p rose and horizons lengthened (link Concept - Trained vs Prompted Agents)
Evidence status: well-documented and reproducible -- the repos, issues, and demos are public
links: Concept - Long-Horizon Agency and Error Compounding
Concept - What Is an LLM Agent

notes.title: Lore - The Devin Demo and the SWE-bench Reality Gap
notes.scope: The March 2024 Devin launch, its SWE-bench claim, and the public teardown that exposed the demo-vs-reality gap. IN: the story, the specific critiques, and the lesson about reading agent numbers. OUT: how SWE-bench is actually built (link Breakdown - SWE-bench and SWE-agent) and eval-methodology rigor (link Concept - Agent Evaluation Challenges).
key_points: What happened: Cognition unveiled Devin (March 2024) as 'the first AI software engineer', claiming ~13.86% on SWE-bench unassisted (beating prior published numbers) alongside a polished autonomous-coding demo; the launch drove a multibillion-dollar valuation narrative

The teardown: Carl Brown's 'Internet of Bugs' video 'Debunking Devin' (April 2024) dissected the flagship Upwork demo -- the task Devin performed did not match the task described, several 'fixes' addressed bugs Devin itself introduced, and the timeline was edited to look smoother than the real run

The lesson: agent launch demos are heavily cherry-picked; a benchmark headline needs its protocol (assisted vs unassisted, Verified subset, pass@k) before it means anything; 'resolved' on SWE-bench is not the same as 'correct and maintainable' (link Concept - Agent Evaluation Challenges)
Broader pattern: the demo-scrutiny cycle repeats with each splashy agent launch; treat a single curated demo as an upper bound, never an expectation
Aftermath: Devin's later general availability drew mixed real-world reviews, consistent with the gap the teardown predicted
Evidence status: the demo, the teardown video, and Cognition's responses are all public; specific intent is contested, the discrepancies are documented
links: Concept - Long-Horizon Agency and Error Compounding

notes.title: Lore - Agent Prompt-Engineering Folklore
notes.scope: The tribal prompting tricks practitioners use to make agents reliable, labeled by whether they are mechanism or cargo cult. IN: recitation, budget signals, format choices, error-as-observation, and the reflection tax. OUT: the underlying context-rot mechanism (link Concept - Context Rot) and the formal loop (link Deep Dive - The Agent Loop).
key_points: Recitation (well-grounded): re-stating the goal or a todo list each turn combats goal drift and lost-in-the-middle over long runs; productized as todo tracking in coding agents (link Concept - Context Rot)
Think-before-acting (grounded): forcing a short reasoning scratchpad before a tool call improves action selection, echoing why ReAct beats act-only (link Concept - The ReAct Pattern)
Budget signals (folklore, weakly sourced): telling the agent 'you have N turns left' to induce urgency/wrap-up; sometimes helps, often ignored
Format lore: XML-tag tool formatting tends to work well with Claude while JSON schemas suit others; partly training-distribution artifact, partly parser-robustness
Error-as-observation (grounded): returning tool exceptions as readable tool results instead of raising lets the model recover instead of crashing the loop
tool_choice forcing (grounded): forcing a call breaks a model that narrates an action instead of emitting it
The reflection tax (grounded caution): over-reflection burns tokens and can entrench errors, matching the self-correction limit (link Concept - Reflection and Self-Correction)
Persona/persistence framing ('do not stop until done') and end-of-turn hygiene: mixed evidence; some is genuine, some cargo cult -- the note's job is to separate them
Evidence status: a mix of mechanistically grounded tricks and labeled folklore drawn from Anthropic/Manus/aider/cursor practitioner writing
links: Concept - Chain-of-Thought and Why It Works

notes.title: Concept - The Lethal Trifecta for Agents
notes.scope: The agent-architecture failure pattern where private-data access, untrusted content, and exfiltration ability combine into data theft, and the defenses. IN: the mechanism, real incidents, and agent-side mitigations. OUT: prompt-injection taxonomy and jailbreak theory (link Concept - Prompt Injection, Concept - Jailbreak Taxonomy), owned by Safety.
key_points: The trifecta (Simon Willison, 2025): an agent that simultaneously (1) can access private/sensitive data, (2) is exposed to untrusted content, and (3) can exfiltrate/communicate externally is a data breach waiting to trigger

Mechanism: injection embedded in untrusted content (a web page, email, file, or MCP tool description) hijacks the agent's instructions; if the same agent can both read secrets and send data out, injection converts directly to exfiltration (link Concept - Prompt Injection)

Real incidents: EchoLeak zero-click data exfiltration in Microsoft 365 Copilot (CVE-2025); the GitHub MCP exploit (Invariant Labs, 2025) where a malicious issue makes the agent leak private-repo contents; Slack AI and ChatGPT-connector exfiltration classes

Defense 1 -- break the trifecta: remove one leg, e.g., no external egress while untrusted content is in context, or no private-data access on untrusted-input paths (link Checklist - Sandboxing an Agent)

Defense 2 -- architectural isolation: the dual-LLM/quarantine pattern (a privileged planner never sees raw untrusted text) and Google's CaMeL (2025) capability-based control separating a trusted planner from tainted data
Defense 3 -- human approval for exfil-capable actions and data-provenance/tainting so untrusted-derived content cannot reach egress unchecked
Ownership boundary: injection/jailbreak taxonomy is Safety's; this note owns the agent-side failure pattern and the practical defenses
Non-obvious: adding a single 'harmless' tool (e.g., outbound web fetch) can complete the trifecta and turn a safe agent dangerous
links: Concept - Tool Use and Function Calling
